endorsements.quote: Rigorous external validation across multiple sites and equipment platforms should become standard practice.
Following standardised AI reporting guidelines, such as TRIPOD+AI, will ensure transparency and reproducibility [ 25 ].
For safe implementation if and when systems mature sufficiently, institutions should start in controlled environments under expert supervision.
Recognise that diagnostic accuracy does not guarantee clinical utility, and maintain physician oversight for all AI-assisted interpretations regardless of the system's reported performance.
Establish clear governance structures defining physician oversight and liability frameworks before deployment.
Only after demonstrating consistent multisite performance should gradual expansion to more challenging environments be considered.
Continuous performance monitoring stratified by patient subgroups is essential, as is creating explicit protocols for handling low-confidence outputs.
AI diagnostic tools must navigate complex approval pathways as "Software as a Medical Device", with regulatory requirements that vary by risk classification.

unlisted_practices: Researchers should conduct prospective trials of AI that include challenging cases rather than excluding them.
Researchers should measure clinical outcomes, not just diagnostic accuracy, in AI studies and report honestly on failure modes and limitations.
Developers should integrate real-time scan quality feedback into AI ultrasound systems to address operator dependency.
Clinicians should demand evidence of external validation across diverse settings and transparency about excluded cases and failure modes before adopting AI.
Institutions should create explicit protocols for handling low-confidence AI outputs.

screen.reason: This is an educational viewpoint/commentary discussing the promise, pitfalls, deployment scenarios, and governance/validation prerequisites for AI in thoracic ultrasound.
